Modules / Carpet

Carpet Cleaning

Pick the condition. Follow the mix. Don't skip the rinse.
1
Level 1 · Maintenance
Normal Cleaning
Routinely vacuumed. Cleaned every 6–12 months.
Method
  1. 1Vacuum (if needed)
  2. 2Yellow tip in 7 scoops of Black Label
  3. 3Agitate with CRB
  4. 4Wand cleaning — 1–2 steam passes with 2–3 dry passes
  5. 5Air mover × 2
  6. 6Groom
Rinse: Fiber Neutralizer · 4 oz per 2 gal · red sprayer
2
Level 2 · Heavily Soiled
Really Dirty
Higher foot traffic. 1+ year since pro clean.
Method
  1. 1Vacuum (if needed)
  2. 2Yellow tip · 7 scoops Black Label · 2 scoops GM
  3. 31 scoop O2 (for lighter carpets)
  4. 48 oz citrus solvent — if grease, deep-set soil, or 3+ years uncleaned
  5. 5Agitate with CRB
  6. 6Wand cleaning — 3+ steam passes followed by 4–5 dry passes
  7. 7Air mover × 2
  8. 8Groom
Rinse: Fiber Neutralizer · 4 oz per 2 gal · red sprayer
3
Level 3 · Restoration
Severely Dirty
Extreme wear. 5+ years uncleaned. Aggressive method.
Method
  1. 1Vacuum if needed ($5 per room)
  2. 2Yellow tip OUT — 1:1 dilution rate
  3. 37 scoops Frog Nasty into Hydroforce with hot water — mix VERY WELL
  4. 4Wait 10 minutes after application
  5. 5Agitate with CRB on traffic areas. Clean edges with wand.
  6. 6Wand cleaning — 3 steam strokes with 4–5 dry strokes (extra dry strokes if needed)
  7. 7Air mover × 2
  8. 8Groom
Rinse: Fiber Neutralizer · 4 oz per 2 gal · red sprayer
Booster options: Citrus solvent — 8 oz per FULL Hydroforce. O2 helps with white or light-colored carpets. Grout Master can be added — 2–4 scoops per full Hydroforce.

Condo Carpets

Method
  1. 1Vacuum (if needed) — vacuum again, sand is embedded
  2. 2Yellow tip · 7 scoops 10K into Hydroforce, mix well
  3. 3Agitate with CRB
  4. 4Wand cleaning — use low PSI wand
  5. 5Air mover · Groom
Rinse: Fiber Neutralizer or Blazing Blue if extremely dirty. Portable: 1 oz/gal fresh tank. Truck mount: 4 oz/2 gal.
If carpets are horrible: 4–8 oz Citrus solvent, 2 scoops GM, 1–2 scoops O2. Don't let detergent dry!

Rentals

Method
  1. 1Vacuum (if needed)
  2. 2Yellow tip · 7 scoops 10K, mix well with hot water
  3. 3Agitate with CRB
  4. 4Normal–medium: 2–4 strokes with equal or greater dry strokes
  5. 5Air mover · Groom
Rinse: Fiber Neutralizer · 4 oz per 2 gal · red sprayer

Commercial (No Pad)

Method
  1. 1Vacuum (if needed)
  2. 2Yellow tip · use Olefin Pre-spray RTU
  3. 3If severely soiled: 10K (7 scoops) with hot water, mix well
  4. 4Agitate with CRB

Method

Technician micro-training · ~7 min

Commercial Glue-Down Carpet

Recognize the installation, understand olefin, and use Fusion's controlled cleaning method.

01 · Identify

Installation and fiber are different facts

Glue-down means the backing is adhered to the floor. Broadloom can cover a room in one continuous sheet. Carpet tiles have visible or hidden seams.

Olefin is polypropylene face fiber. Commercial glued carpet may instead use nylon, polyester, or a blend. Confirm the fiber through labels or site records when available — or use the Textile ID module.

Inspect loose seams, damaged backing, stains and traffic lanes before applying chemistry.
02 · Recognize

Where you may find it

Low pile commercial carpet appears in offices, churches, corridors, waiting rooms, and some hospital administrative spaces. Each site may use a different fiber and backing.

Office corridorsCompact loops and oily traffic lanes.
ChurchesHigh traffic aisles and entry areas.
Clinics & officesCheck access, drying time and building rules.
03 · Fiber behavior

What olefin means on the job

  • Resists water absorption — polypropylene takes up little water and resists many water-based stains.
  • Attracts oily soil — body oils, asphalt residue and other oily soil cling to traffic lanes.
  • Low pile holds grit — dry particles pack near the backing. Vacuuming first matters.
The fiber's water resistance does not protect the backing, adhesive or floor beneath it from excess moisture.
04 · Fusion procedure

A controlled, efficient cleaning sequence

  1. 1Inspect and vacuum. Note seams, backing condition, spots and traffic lanes. Remove dry soil.
  2. 2Apply Fusion-approved olefin pre-spray. Follow the label for dilution and dwell. Avoid pooling or letting it dry.
  3. 3Agitate when needed. Focus on packed or oily soil without damaging the pile.
  4. 4Extract in straight lanes. Begin with one slightly overlapping wet pass on normally soiled carpet.
05 · Finish and protect

Fast does not mean flooded

  • Check soil removal, moisture and recovery after the first pass. Add a dry pass where needed, especially near edges or heavier soil.
  • Avoid repeated wet strokes and standing moisture. Use airflow and follow the site's access requirements.
  • Use solvent spotters sparingly, only when compatible. Keep them out of the backing — some solvents weaken backing or adhesive.
  • If seams lift, backing softens, or moisture pools — stop and notify the crew lead.
Field rule: Low pile glue-down often cleans faster than plush carpet, but the installation and soil condition decide the pace and number of passes.

Knowledge Check · 4 of 5 to pass

1. What does “glue-down” identify?
2. Which soil can cling strongly to olefin?
3. What comes before pre-spray?
4. Starting extraction approach on normally soiled, sound low pile carpet?
5. A seam begins lifting during cleaning. What do you do?

Carpet cleaning booster that blows through thick greasy grout lines. Add 1–2 scoops to your current prespray inline sprayer mix — works on rat-nasties. Safe for residential and commercial. Also a strong prespray booster for polyesters.

Understanding Carpet Dirt Levels

A quick read on what the customer's carpet is actually telling you.

1
Regularly Soiled · Normal Dirty
Standard day-to-day accumulation. Vacuumed at least weekly and professionally cleaned every 6–12 months. This is routine maintenance.
2
Heavily Soiled · Really Dirty
Higher-than-normal foot traffic, or hasn't been professionally cleaned in over a year. Vacuuming may be inconsistent. Visible dirt buildup and traffic-area wear are common.
3
Severely Soiled · Extreme Cases
Not cleaned in 5+ years, extreme traffic wear, poor or nonexistent vacuuming. Buildup includes deep-set grime, odors, and staining — often requires aggressive restoration techniques.

Dirty Carpet Edges (Filtration Soiling)

Dark lines along walls or under doors? That's filtration soiling — dirty air moving through gaps and getting trapped in the carpet fibers. Usually linked to the HVAC system.

If routine cleaning doesn't resolve it, a specialized Filter Edge Treatment may be needed. Pricing varies by severity. Recommend regular HVAC filter changes to prevent it returning.
Modules / Textile ID

Textile Identification

IICRC S100 / S300 fiber ID — visual, burn, and bleach tests.
Why this matters
Wrong chemistry on the wrong fiber = damage, complaint, claim. IICRC standards require fiber ID before cleaning. Always pull samples from a hidden area — under cushions, inside seams, behind furniture, or rug fringe.

Visual & Tactile Pre-Check

First pass before any chemical work. Look and feel.

  • Sheen — natural fibers are usually matte. Synthetics often have a sheen.
  • Hand feel — wool is springy and warm. Cotton soft and cool. Polyester smooth and slick. Olefin waxy. Silk fine and slippery.
  • Construction — jute backing or hand-knotted = natural. Tufted with synthetic backing = synthetic.
  • Fiber length — short staple suggests wool or cotton. Long filament suggests synthetic.

Quick Tells by Fiber

A starting point — confirm with burn or bleach when stakes are high.

FiberWhat you see / feel
WoolDull finish, crimpy, springy, warm
Cotton / LinenMatte, soft, no sheen
SilkHigh natural luster, very fine, slippery
NylonBright color retention, durable, slight sheen
PolyesterSilky sheen, soft hand
OlefinWaxy feel, no static, common in Berber
AcrylicWool-like look, lighter weight, softer
Safety first. Pull a few strands from a hidden area (seam allowance, under cushion). Use tweezers, work over a non-flammable surface or sink with water nearby. Good ventilation, no flammables nearby.

What to observe

Four things — and they tell you almost everything.

  1. 1How it burns — fast, slow, melts, self-extinguishes
  2. 2Smell — paper, hair, plastic, celery, candle wax
  3. 3Smoke — color and amount
  4. 4Residue — soft ash, crushable bead, or hard plastic bead
C
Category 1 · Natural Cellulose
Cotton · Linen · Rayon · Jute
Burns
Fast, steady flame
Smell
Burning paper or leaves
Residue
Light gray, soft ash that crumbles between fingers
P
Category 2 · Natural Protein
Wool · Silk
Burns
Slow, often self-extinguishes
Smell
Burning hair or feathers
Residue
Black, crushable bead at the tip
S
Category 3 · Synthetic
Nylon · Polyester · Olefin · Acrylic

All synthetics melt before burning, drip, smell chemical, and leave a hard plastic bead.

Specifics
FiberBurnSmellBead
NylonMelts, self-extinguishesCelery-likeHard, gray/tan

Chlorine Bleach Solubility Test

Use this when the burn test points to natural protein and you need to confirm wool before locking in your chemistry.

Procedure
  1. 1Pull a small fiber sample from a hidden area
  2. 2Drop into a small container of full-strength liquid chlorine bleach
  3. 3Wait 15–20 minutes
  4. 4Read the result below

Reading the Result

After 15–20 minutes, look at what's left in the container.

✓
Wool / Silk DISSOLVES COMPLETELY
Bleach destroys protein bonds. Treat as wool. pH 5–8 only, no chlorine, no high heat, gentle agitation, Fiber Neutralizer rinse.
—
Cotton / Cellulose STAYS INTACT
Stays intact, may discolor. Not protein.
—
Synthetics NO CHANGE
Stays intact, no change. Confirm specific synthetic via burn test.
Safety: Wear gloves. Work in ventilation. Don't mix bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners.

Once you know the fiber, here's what to do — and what not to do.

W

Wool / Silk

  • pH 5–8 only — neutral to slightly acidic
  • Never high-alkaline detergents
  • Never chlorine bleach
  • Never hot water
  • Fiber Neutralizer rinse · air dry
C

Cotton / Linen

  • Watch for cellulose browning
  • Dry quickly to prevent wicking
  • Browning treatment if needed
N

Nylon

  • Most durable — wider pH range
  • Standard protocols apply
  • Stain-resistant treatments may not tolerate high pH
P

Polyester

  • Oleophilic — loves oils
  • Citrus solvent & oil-cutting boosters work well
  • Standard protocols
O

Olefin

  • Bleach-stable
  • Heat-sensitive — never high heat
  • Citrus solvent essential for grease
  • Common in Berber and outdoor
A

Acrylic

  • Heat-sensitive — keep temps moderate
  • Standard pH range OK
EVERY TEXTILE JOB
Always
  • Colorfastness check before any cleaner — white towel blot test
  • Document fiber ID in the job notes
  • When in doubt, treat it as the most delicate fiber it could be
  • IICRC S100 and S300 require fiber ID — your protection in a damage claim
Modules / Spotting

Spotting Guide

Bridgepoint Spot & Stain Removal Kit · 5 categories.
Before you start
Pretest in a hidden area first. Work outside-in to prevent spreading. Don't over-apply. Tamp, don't scrub. Finish every job with Spot Stop to prevent wicking and re-soiling.
1
Synthetic Color & Dye
Kool-Aid · children's red medicine · fruit punch · sports drinks
Procedure
  1. 1Apply Red Zone Ready — enough to thoroughly wet the stain but not soak the backing
  2. 2Lay wet cotton towel (usually double thickness) over stain. Apply heated iron at lowest steam setting. Quick check every 20–30 seconds
  3. 3When color is gone, a yellow cast usually remains. Rinse thoroughly
  4. 4Mist Spot Stop and work in with the Whiz Groom
2
Organic Stains & Natural Dyes
Urine · decaffeinated coffee · mold · wood stains
Procedure
  1. 1Apply Stain Zone to contaminated area
  2. 2Lightly agitate and allow to dwell until stain is gone
  3. 3If stain is gone, extract rinse. Otherwise Stain Zone self-neutralizes with no re-soiling and continues working until it dries
3
Oil, Resin or Pigmented
Ink · grease · cosmetics · adhesives · polish · gum
Ink & Marker
  1. 1Apply Avenge Pro directly to stain, agitate, dwell 30 seconds
  2. 2Dry extract with vac tool, repeat if needed
  3. 3Apply All Solv Extreme · agitate · then Avenge Pro · agitate
  4. 4Rinse and mist with Spot Stop
Fingernail Polish

Critical containment trick: apply Avenge Pro AROUND the stain first. It blocks All Solv Extreme and dissolved pigment from wicking into the backing. Avenge Pro doesn't "set" stains — it's safe to lead with.

  1. 1Apply Avenge Pro around the contaminated area (not on it) to guard against wicking
  2. 2Apply All Solv Extreme, lightly agitate, absorb pigment into a white towel. Repeat until most pigment is gone
  3. 3Apply Avenge Pro and agitate lightly
  4. 4Rinse and mist Spot Stop, work in with Whiz Groom
Gum (chewing)
  1. 1Poke holes in gum surface with the Gum Getter
  2. 2Apply Gel Break to surface, dwell 5–10 minutes
  3. 3Agitate and remove gum with the Gum Getter into a towel. Repeat as needed. For residue: apply small amount of Gel Break, agitate with towel, then rinse thoroughly with water
  4. 4Mist Spot Stop and work in with Whiz Groom
4
Protein & Most Food Spills
Blood · egg · chocolate sauce · most food
Procedure
  1. 1Remove excess contaminant (blot, scrape, vacuum)
  2. 2Apply Avenge Pro and agitate. If hard, allow Avenge Pro to dwell and soften the contaminant
  3. 3Rinse and repeat if necessary
  4. 4Mist Spot Stop and work in with Whiz Groom
Note: Some food stains contain synthetic or organic dyes. If stain remains after the above, vacuum dry and follow Cat 1 (Red Zone Ready) for synthetic dyes or Cat 2 (Stain Zone) for organic dyes.
5
Specialty Stains
Rust · yellowing · water stains
Procedure
  1. 1Apply T-Rust
  2. 2Lightly agitate and allow to dwell until stain disappears
  3. 3Rinse thoroughly
Note: Some yellowing and water stains may also respond to Stain Zone. For unknown specialty stains, see the Unknown tab.

Use the Unknown tab procedure — work the kit in order: Avenge Pro → All Solv Extreme → Stain Zone or Red Zone Ready (test which).

Unknown Stain Procedure

When the stain origin is unknown, work the kit in this order. Avenge Pro doesn't "set" stains — it's always safe to lead with.

1
Apply Avenge Pro · agitate
If stain is releasing → continue and rinse
2
If stain remains: Apply All Solv Extreme · agitate
If releasing → continue, then apply Avenge Pro, rinse
3
If stain remains: Apply Stain Zone OR Red Zone Ready
Origin is unknown → test in a hidden area to determine which works
EVERY SPOT JOB
Always
  • Pretest any solution in a hidden area before using on the visible stain
  • Remove excess (blot, scrape, vacuum) before applying liquid
  • Work from outside edges to center to prevent spreading
  • Tamp, don't scrub. Aggressive scrubbing causes texture change ("fuzzy carpet")
  • Don't over-apply — too much chemical spreads the stain and damages backing
  • Be patient. Most spotters need dwell time. Let chemistry do the work
  • Finish every job with Spot Stop — encapsulates residue, prevents re-soiling

The 7 chemicals and the agitation tools in the Bridgepoint Pro Kit.

Avenge Pro

Universal · Water-based

The most versatile spotter. Lead with this on Cat 3, 4, and Unknown. Won't "set" stains — safe to use first on virtually anything organic, oil-based, or food.

All Solv Extreme

Gelled solvent

Used in Cat 3 (oils, resins, polish, ink). Always after Avenge Pro — Avenge Pro contains the spread, then All Solv lifts the pigment.

Gel Break

Gum & adhesive solvent

Specialty solvent for gum, adhesives, and sticky residue. 5–10 minute dwell. Used with the Gum Getter tool.

Stain Zone

Organic stain remover · Cat 2

For organic stains and natural dyes (urine, coffee, mold, wood). Self-neutralizes on the carpet — no re-soiling, keeps working until it dries.

Red Zone Ready

Synthetic dye remover · Cat 1

For synthetic dye stains (Kool-Aid, fruit punch, red medicine). Requires heat — apply through wet cotton towel with a heated iron. Yellow cast usually remains; rinse thoroughly.

T-Rust

Specialty · Cat 5

Acidic rust remover. Apply, dwell until stain disappears, rinse thoroughly.

Spot Stop

Encapsulating · Anti-wicking

The final step on every job. Encapsulates residue, drives it under the fiber, prevents re-soiling and wicking. Misted on, worked in with the Whiz Groom.

Kit Tools & Contents

What ships in the Bridgepoint Pro Kit alongside the chemicals.

  • Gum Getter — agitation tool for poking holes in gum and scraping spent residue
  • Whiz Groom — agitation tool used after Spot Stop, works the encapsulant into the fiber
  • White cotton towels — for blotting and pigment absorption
  • Nitrile gloves — 3 pair
  • Insulated carry bag — keeps chemicals at temperature, big enough for extras

Modules / Tile & Grout

Tile, Stone & Grout

IICRC Stone, Masonry & Ceramic Tile (SMT) training reference.
Goal: Identify the surface type correctly — the #1 rule of the SMT technician.

The Two Families of Natural Stone

Every stone job starts with this question. Get it wrong and you can destroy a floor.

Family 1

Calcareous

Made of calcium carbonate. Soft, porous, destroyed by acids — even vinegar or lemon juice etches it.

⚠ Never use acid
Marble · Limestone · Travertine · Onyx
Family 2

Siliceous

Made of silicates & quartz. Harder and generally acid-resistant, but acid cleaners still aren't recommended.

✓ Test first
Granite · Slate · Sandstone · Quartzite

Man-Made Surfaces

  • Ceramic tile — fired clay with a glaze. Durable surface; the weak point is the grout.
  • Porcelain tile — denser, less porous ceramic. Very chemical-tolerant.
  • Cementitious grout — porous like a sponge; absorbs soil and stains. Sanded vs. unsanded matters for agitation.
  • Engineered quartz — uniform speckle, resin warmth. Ruined by high heat and harsh solvents (but not by acids).
  • Cultured marble — gel-coat over resin. Treat it like plastic — never abrasives or acids.

Field ID · Natural vs. Man-Made

Six quick checks. Two answers side by side.

Pattern
Every tile is unique — veining runs THROUGH the material
Patterns repeat — find two identical tiles and it's printed
Edges & back
Same material all the way through; sawn or honed edges
Glazed face over clay body (different color under); molded back
Touch & temp
Feels cold and dense; polished stone shows crystal grain
Glaze feels glassy; resin (quartz) feels warmer, slightly plastic
Water drop
Unsealed stone darkens as it absorbs (limestone, travertine)
Glazed tile and quartz shed water — no darkening
Scratch test
Marble/limestone scratch with a knife; granite resists
Glaze resists scratching; deep scratch reveals clay body
Acid drop
Fizzes on calcareous stone
No reaction on the glaze
Field tip: Not sure? A scratch test (calcareous is softer) or acid-drop test in a hidden spot tells you. Calcareous fizzes. When in doubt, treat it as calcareous — the safe assumption.

Pop Quiz · Surfaces

1. Marble and travertine belong to which stone family?
2. A customer mopped their marble floor with vinegar. What happened?
3. On a ceramic tile floor, which part absorbs the most soil?
4. A "marble" floor where several tiles have identical veining patterns is most likely…
Goal: Match the cleaner's pH to the soil — and to the surface.

The Working Rules

Acids dissolve minerals. Alkalines dissolve grease & oils. Neutral is safe on everything.

2–4
Acidic
Hard water · scale · efflorescence · grout haze
7
Neutral
Daily stone care · won't strip sealers
9–12
Alkaline
Grease · oils · heavy soil · restoration

The pH Scale (Visual)

What's Actually in the Bottle

pH is only half the story. Two alkaline degreasers at the same pH can perform completely differently depending on what else is inside.

IngredientJobWhere it matters
SurfactantsLower surface tension so solution wets into pores; suspend loosened soilPorous grout & stone — also why thorough rinsing matters
Builders / alkaline saltsRaise pH, saponify fats and oilsKitchen grease, traffic film
Chelating agentsGrab hard-water minerals so they don't redepositHard-water areas; lets you clean scale without acid
SolventsDissolve oily & greasy soils chemistry alone won't touchInk, tar, adhesive — but can dull resin surfaces and epoxy grout
Oxidizers / peroxideBreak down organic color — coffee, wine, biological growthGrout stains; always test for color loss first
Read the label, not the marketing. "Safe for stone" on the front means nothing without a pH figure and a dilution ratio on the back. If a product won't tell you its pH, don't put it on someone's marble.
Safety: Never mix chemicals. Acid + bleach or ammonia + bleach creates toxic gas. Always ventilate, gloves and eye protection on, follow the SDS. High-pH strippers burn skin just like acids do.

Pop Quiz · Chemistry

1. Greasy restaurant kitchen quarry tile. Which chemistry?
2. Hard-water scale on a porcelain shower. Best choice?
3. Everyday maintenance cleaner for ALL natural stone?
Goal: A proper pre-job inspection prevents 90% of damage claims.

The Pre-Job Walkthrough

  1. 1Identify the surface (Surface tab skills) and the soil type (Chemistry tab skills)
  2. 2Document existing damage — cracked tiles, missing/loose grout, chips, lippage, hollow-sounding tiles. Photograph and show the customer before starting
  3. 3Stain vs. etch — a stain is IN the stone (absorbed, darker). An etch is damage TO the stone (acid burn, dull/lighter). Cleaning removes stains; etching needs honing/polishing
  4. 4Test in an inconspicuous area — chemical, temperature, and pressure. Every time. No exceptions
  5. 5Set expectations — permanently stained grout may need colorant, not just cleaning. Say it up front

Stain vs. Etch

Different problems. Different fixes. Know the difference before you promise anything.

Problem 1

Stain

Something in the stone. Absorbed. Usually appears darker. Comes from spills, food, oils, urine.
Fix: clean or poultice
Problem 2

Etch

Damage to the stone. Appears lighter, dull ring or spot. Caused by acid contact — vinegar, wine, citrus, soft drinks.
Fix: honing / polishing
Remember: If you clean over pre-existing damage without documenting it, YOU own that damage in the customer's eyes. Photos + walkthrough = protection.

Pop Quiz · Inspection

1. A dull, lighter ring on a marble counter where a glass sat is a…
2. Where should you test your cleaning solution first?
3. You spot cracked tiles before starting. What do you do?
Goal: Follow the professional SMT sequence. Chemistry does the work — the machine finishes it.

The SMT Six-Step Sequence

Same order. Every job.

1
Dry Soil Removal — vacuum / sweep
Wet cleaning over grit = mud + scratches
2
Apply Solution — correct chemistry, correct dilution
Follow label dilution — more is NOT better
3
Dwell — 5 to 15 minutes, keep wet
Chemistry needs time to break soil bonds. Skipping dwell is the #1 rookie mistake
4
Agitate — rotary brush or grout brush
Mechanical action lifts soil from the pores
5
Rinse & Extract — hot water extraction or spinner tool
Removes soil AND residue. Repeat until water runs clear
6
Dry & Inspect — air movers, final walkthrough
Prevents slips; confirms results with the customer

C.H.A.T. — The Four Dials You Control

Every job balances four factors. Turn one down and you have to turn another up. This is what separates a technician from someone pushing a machine.

C
Chemical
Breaks the bond between soil and surface
Turn down for: delicate stone, sealed surfaces, food-prep areas — compensate with time and agitation
H
Heat
Speeds the reaction — roughly doubles activity every 18°F
Turn down for: waxes & coatings (they soften), resin surfaces, radiant-heated floors
A
Agitation
Mechanically lifts soil out of pores and texture
Turn down for: soft grout, polished stone, cleft slate with loose flakes
T
Time
Dwell — lets chemistry finish the work
Rarely turn down. Time is the free dial, and it's the one rookies skip
Use it as a decision tool. Polished marble means C and A both come down — so H and T go up. Restaurant quarry tile can take all four wide open. Say the trade-off out loud before you start.

Tool Selection

Rotary machine with brush
Best for
Textured tile, slate, wide grout networks
Watch
Brush stiffness — too aggressive scars soft grout & polished stone
Spinner / enclosed pressure tool
Best for
Large open ceramic & porcelain floors
Watch
Contain the spray; cap pressure over soft or failing grout
Hand grout brush
Best for
Edges, corners, detail work, shower walls
Watch
Slow — budget the time honestly in the estimate
White or red pads
Best for
Polished stone, honed surfaces
Watch
Never move up to black or green on polished stone
Air movers
Best for
Every job, always
Watch
Not optional — dry time is part of the service

How Do You Know the Rinse Is Done?

  • Rinse water comes back clear, not tinted or foamy
  • Wipe a dry white towel across a dried section — it should come up clean, no film
  • On alkaline jobs, a pH strip in the rinse water reading near neutral tells you the chemistry is out
  • A haze appearing as the floor dries is residue, not soil. Rinse again — don't reach for more product
Equipment & safety: Cap pressure on stone and soft grout (high PSI blows out grout). Contain overspray, mask baseboards and cabinets, post wet-floor signs. PPE: gloves, eye protection, slip-resistant boots.

Pop Quiz · Process

1. What must happen BEFORE any wet cleaning?
2. Why does the cleaning solution need dwell time?
3. The floor still looks hazy after cleaning. Most likely cause?
Goal: Finish the job right. Turn one cleaning into a maintenance program.

Two Kinds of Sealers

Standard choice

Penetrating (Impregnating)

Soaks INTO the pores. Repels oil and water. Keeps the natural look. Lets the stone breathe.

✓ Standard for stone & grout
Use with caution

Topical (Coating)

Sits ON the surface. Adds gloss. Can trap moisture, scuff, and require stripping when it fails.

⚠ Caution on natural stone

Sealing Rules

  • Surface must be clean and fully dry — typically 24–48 hrs after deep cleaning for grout
  • Sealers buy reaction time, they don't make stone stain-proof. Spills still need prompt wipe-up
  • Efflorescence (white mineral powder) = moisture moving through the material. Fix the moisture source, don't just seal over it
WEEK 1 RECAP

The Five Golden Rules

  • MONIdentify the surface first — calcareous vs. siliceous
  • TUEMatch pH to the soil AND the surface. Acids never touch marble
  • WEDInspect, document, test in a hidden spot — every job
  • THUVacuum → apply → dwell → agitate → extract → dry
  • FRISeal clean, dry surfaces. Sealers buy time, not immunity

Pop Quiz · Sealing

1. Which sealer keeps the natural look and lets stone breathe?
2. How long should grout typically dry after deep cleaning before sealing?
3. A sealed granite counter gets a wine spill. True statement?
Goal: Know what grout you're standing on. It decides your chemistry, pressure, and whether it needs sealing.

The Four Grout Types

Sanded Cementitious
Porous
Cement + sand
Used in
Joints 1/8" and wider — most floors
Cleaning
Absorbs soil, needs sealing. Tolerates agitation well
Unsanded Cementitious
Porous
Cement, no sand
Used in
Joints under 1/8" — walls, polished stone (sand would scratch)
Cleaning
Softer than sanded. Gentler agitation, lower pressure. Needs sealing
Epoxy
Non-porous
Resin + hardener
Used in
Commercial kitchens, showers, countertops
Cleaning
Stain-proof, no sealer needed. Strong solvents can dull it
Urethane / Pre-Mixed
Non-porous
Ready-to-use polymer
Used in
Residential re-grouts
Cleaning
No sealer needed. Avoid harsh solvents and prolonged soaking

How Grout Is Installed

Why it matters to cleaners.

  • Mix & slake — cementitious grout is mixed, rested (~10 min), remixed. Too much water = weak, powdery grout that crumbles under aggressive cleaning
  • Float & pack — pressed diagonally into joints with a rubber float. Poorly packed joints leave voids — they trap soil and blow out under high pressure
  • Sponge & haze — excess sponged off; leftover film is grout haze. Cement haze on ceramic can take a mild acid haze remover — never on marble
  • Cure — cement grout cures ~28 days to full strength. Light cleaning only for the first 48–72 hrs. Sealer per manufacturer
  • Why you care — crumbling grout = installation or water problem, not a cleaning problem. Document it and quote a re-grout or colorant instead of over-scrubbing
Field check: Drop water on the grout. Darkens fast → porous cementitious, unsealed → needs sealing after cleaning. Beads up → sealed, epoxy, or urethane → cleaning only, skip the sealer pitch.

Pop Quiz · Grout

1. Which grout joints get UNSANDED grout?
2. Which grout type never needs sealing?
3. Grout crumbles as you agitate. What's the right move?
4. Water drops bead up on the grout line. What does that tell you?
Goal: Recognize the jobs that need restoration, moisture control, or a different trade — before you turn the machine on.

Etch Repair — Honing & Polishing

Cleaning never fixes an etch. The stone surface is physically dissolved — remove material until the damage is gone, then rebuild the finish.

Light etch
water spots · polished marble
Marble polishing powder + white pad, low speed, water
Gloss restored in minutes; spot repair blends
Moderate etch
dull traffic lanes
Hone with fine diamonds (400 → 800 → 1500 → 3000), then polish
Full section restored — blend to a grout line or wall
Deep etch
scratches · lippage
Grind with coarse diamonds (50 → 100 → 200) then work up the grit chain
Restoration job, not a cleaning job — price it separately
Grit rule: never skip more than one grit step. Each pass only removes the scratch pattern of the pass before it — jumping grits leaves a haze you cannot polish out, and you end up starting over.

Stain Removal — The Poultice

An absorbent powder + the right chemical mixed to peanut-butter paste. It sits on the stain and pulls it back out of the stone as it dries.

Match the chemical to the stain
  • Oil / grease → degreaser or acetone
  • Organic (coffee, wine, leaf) → hydrogen peroxide
  • Ink / dye → solvent
  • Biological growth → peroxide-based cleaner
Method
  1. 1Pre-wet the stone with water
  2. 2Apply paste about ¼" thick and 1" past the stain edge
  3. 3Cover with plastic, tape the edges, dwell 24–48 hours
  4. 4Uncover and let dry completely — the drying is what lifts the stain
  5. 5Scrape off, rinse, repeat if the stain lightened but didn't clear
Expectations: deep old stains often take three or four cycles, and some never leave completely. Say so up front.
Careful: most rust removers are acidic. On marble, limestone, or travertine they will etch while they work on the rust — you trade a stain for permanent damage. Rust in calcareous stone is usually a restoration referral, not a cleaning task.

Over-Wetting — Damage After the Floor Looks Great

Tile is waterproof. The assembly underneath usually isn't. Flooding a floor sends water where it can't dry.

Tile over wood subfloor / upper floors
Water through grout swells the subfloor; can leak to the ceiling below
Low-moisture method, tight passes, extract immediately, air movers
Showers & wet rooms
Old pans and failed membranes leak into walls and framing
Control volume, never pressure-blast joints, dry aggressively
Missing/damaged grout, hollow tiles
Open path straight to the setting bed
Document, avoid, and quote repair first
Cabinet toe kicks, thresholds, carpet transitions
Wicking into cabinetry and carpet pad
Mask and dam edges; keep solution off transitions
Radiant heat under tile
Fast evaporation locks residue in; hot surfaces flash chemistry
Turn the system down, work small sections, rinse thoroughly

Efflorescence

White powdery bloom on grout, pavers, and stone. It's soluble mineral salt — moisture travels through the assembly, dissolves salts, carries them to the surface, and leaves them as the water evaporates. Moisture symptom, not soil.

  • Remove it dry first — vacuum and brush. Wetting it just redissolves and redeposits
  • Residual haze on acid-tolerant surfaces can take a diluted acidic cleaner, followed by a thorough neutral rinse. Never on calcareous stone
  • If you don't stop the moisture — leaking irrigation, no vapor barrier, grade against the building — it comes straight back. Say so before you seal anything over it

Slip Resistance — Your Biggest Liability After the Truck Leaves

  • Residue is slippery. Incomplete rinsing leaves surfactant film that gets dangerous the first time it's wet again
  • Industry benchmark for level interior floors expected to get wet is a wet dynamic coefficient of friction (DCOF) of 0.42 or higher under ANSI A326.3. Polished stone and topical gloss coatings can fall below it
  • Adding a high-gloss coating to a commercial floor without a traction additive can turn a clean floor into a claim. Ask what the space is used for before you propose gloss
  • Wet-floor signs stay up until you've confirmed the floor is dry — not until you're done cleaning
0.42 The DCOF standard. ANSI A326.3 minimum for wet interior floors. Below this and the floor is legally slippery.

Movement Joints, Caulk & Hollow Tile

  • Every change of plane — wall to floor, inside corners, tub and counter edges — should be flexible sealant, not grout. Cracked grout in a corner is a design failure, not dirt
  • Cracking in a straight line across a floor usually means a missing movement joint or a moving substrate. Cleaning won't change it — aggressive cleaning will widen it
  • Tap-test suspect areas. A hollow sound means the tile has debonded from the substrate. Note it, photograph it, avoid it — pressure will pop it loose and it becomes your tile
  • Mold in a shower: black growth on the surface of silicone usually means the sealant is colonized underneath and needs replacing. Bleach lightens the color and leaves the problem
The professional move: pre-existing conditions are a sales opportunity, not a problem to hide. "I found three things I want to show you before I start" builds more trust than a perfect-looking invoice ever will — and it puts repair work on the estimate.

1 · Identify the Surface

If you see…It's probably…Chemistry ceiling

Muted earthy tone, fossil flecksLimestone — calcareousNeutral only

When you can't tell: treat it as calcareous and treat it as coated. Both assumptions are the conservative one. You can always step up; you can never un-etch a floor.

SoilChemistryOnly if surface is…
Routine maintenance, light trafficNeutral pH 7Anything
Kitchen grease, body oils, traffic filmAlkaline pH 9–12Tile, grout, most stone (test polished)

Wax, acrylic finish, failed topical sealerStripper (high pH or solvent)Per coating manufacturer; mask everything
Organic growth, mildew stainPeroxide / oxidizerTest for color loss first, always

3 · Mix It Right

Dilution written as 1 part product : X parts water. Measure it — eyeballing costs more in product and leaves residue.

LabelPer 1 gallonPer 5-gal tank
1:426 oz128 oz (1 gal)
1:814 oz71 oz
1:167.5 oz38 oz
1:324 oz19 oz
1:642 oz10 oz
1:1281 oz5 oz
Stronger is not faster. Over-concentrated solution dries faster, leaves more residue, takes extra rinse passes. If soil isn't coming up, add dwell or agitation before you add product.

4 · Pre-Job Walkthrough

Tap to check off each item as you go.

  • Surface identified — calcareous, siliceous, or man-made

  • Floor dried with air movers; edges and corners checked

6 · The Never List
  • Acid on marble, limestone, travertine, or onyx

Modules / Oriental Rugs

Oriental & Area Rugs

IICRC Rug Cleaning Technician (RCT) principles · ANSI/IICRC S100.
Rule #1 of rug cleaning

Know the construction and fiber before anything gets wet

A rug is a textile, not a floor. Construction and fiber decide the method, the chemistry and the risk.

Four Construction Types

Flip the corner. The back tells you more than the front.

  • Hand-knotted — each knot tied around the warp threads. Design shows clearly on the back with visible individual knots. Fringe is the warp itself, not sewn on. Slight irregularities in size and pattern.
  • Hand-tufted — yarn punched through a canvas, held by latex glue, covered with a cloth backing. Back is covered; fringe is sewn or glued on. Latex breaks down with age, water and heat.
  • Machine-made — two kinds. Machine-woven (power-loomed): pile woven into the backing, perfect grid on the back. Machine-tufted: tufts glued with latex to a mesh or jute backing — basically carpet with bound edges. Fringe usually sewn on. See the Backings tab.
  • Flatweave (kilim, dhurrie, soumak) — no pile, often reversible. Cotton or wool. High risk for dye bleeding and shrinkage.

Visual Reference

Hand-knotted
Natural fibers
Pattern slightly irregular, fringe from warp
Back & fringe
Key ID check
Design mirrors the front, knots visible
Wool pile
Protein fiber
Dense, matte, springy
Kilim / flatweave
No pile
Reversible, bleed & shrink risk
Hand-knotting loom
How it's made
Every knot tied by hand around warps

Fiber — Pile and Foundation

Test both. The face yarn and the foundation (warp & weft) are often different fibers. Use the Textile ID module burn and bleach tests.

FiberWhere you find itWhat it means for you
WoolMost Oriental rug pileWool-safe chemistry, no high alkalinity, no chlorine, no excess heat
SilkFine pile, highlights, fringeVery delicate — water marks, dye bleed, pile distortion. Specialist job
CottonFoundation, fringe, flatweavesBrowns, shrinks and yellows if over-wet or dried slowly
Viscose / rayonSold as “art silk,” “bamboo silk,” “banana silk”Loses strength wet, distorts, browns, yellows. Highest-risk rug you'll see
JuteBackings, natural-look rugsBrowns and weakens when wet — keep moisture low
SyntheticsMachine-made rugsMost forgiving; olefin still holds oily soil

Find the Nap

Hand-knotted pile leans one direction. Run your hand end to end — the smooth direction is with the nap.

  • Wash, extract and groom with the nap
  • Rugs look lighter viewed with the nap and darker against it — explain this to customers who think an area didn't clean

Pop Quiz · Identify

1. Fringe is part of the warp threads, and the design shows clearly on the back. What is it?
2. A customer says her rug is “bamboo silk.” What's the actual fiber?
3. The back of a rug is covered with a glued cloth. What should you expect?
Goal: Know what is holding the rug together. The backing decides how much water, heat and agitation the rug can take.

The Flip Test

Turn a corner over in good light and match what you see.

Back looks like…It is…Wet-cleaning risk
Design mirrors the front, individual knots, slightly irregularHand-knottedLow–moderate (test dyes)
Design visible in a tight, perfect grid; maybe light stiff coatingMachine-woven (power-loomed)Low–moderate
Covered by a glued cloth (often cotton canvas); edges bound; fringe sewn onHand-tuftedHigh — latex & trapped moisture
Even woven mesh (polypropylene) or brown jute; bound or serged edgesMachine-tuftedModerate — high if jute
No back — same on both sidesFlatweaveModerate (bleed, shrink)

Cross-Sections — What's Inside

Hand-Knotted

No backing

Knots tied around warp threads, locked in by wefts. Nothing is glued. This is why hand-knotted rugs can be fully washed.

Hand-Tufted

Latex + cloth

Yarn is shot through a primary cloth with a tufting gun. Latex on the back is the only thing holding the tufts. A secondary cloth is glued over it to hide the latex.

Machine-Tufted

Latex + mesh

Same idea as hand-tufted, made by machine — basically a piece of carpet with bound edges. Secondary backing is woven polypropylene (stable) or jute (browns, shrinks, weak when wet).

Machine-Woven

Woven in

Pile is woven into the backing on a power loom (Wilton / Axminster style). No latex layer holding tufts, but many have a light back sizing to stiffen them.

Hand-Tufted Rugs — What You Need to Know

The most common "Oriental-look" rug in homes today, and the one most likely to cause problems.

  • Latex ages. After several years it dries, cracks and turns to powder. You'll see dust coming out the back, stiffness, and crackling when you fold a corner
  • Odor. Old latex can give off a sour or chemical smell when wet — it is not always pet urine
  • Delamination. The secondary cloth separates from the latex, creating bubbles, ripples and buckling
  • Shedding and loose tufts. As latex fails, tufts pull out — often mistaken for "bad cleaning"
  • Trapped moisture. Water sits between the two layers and dries slowly, which leads to browning, odor and brown stains wicking up from the latex and cloth
  • Urine gets trapped between the backing layers. Full decontamination is often not possible — say so up front
  • Many are made with viscose pile (see Identify) — double the risk
Cleaning approach: thorough dusting and vacuuming, low moisture, minimal heat, gentle agitation, extra dry passes, fast drying with airflow on both sides. Never flood or soak a hand-tufted rug.

Machine-Tufted Rugs — What You Need to Know

  • Usually synthetic pile (nylon, polyester, olefin) — clean much like carpet, but off the floor
  • Polypropylene mesh backing — stable, tolerates normal hot water extraction
  • Jute backing — browns and shrinks when over-wet. Low moisture, acid rinse, dry fast
  • Edges are bound or serged — binding tape can shrink, bleed or pull away if soaked
  • Remnants cut from wall-to-wall carpet fall in this category
Corner fold test: gently fold a back corner. Crackling, powder, or a stiff "cardboard" feel means the latex is breaking down — document it and warn the customer before cleaning.

Pop Quiz · Backings

1. You flip a rug and the back is covered by a glued canvas cloth, fringe sewn on. What is it?
2. What holds the tufts in a hand-tufted rug?
3. Powder falls out and the corner crackles when folded. What's happening?
4. A machine-tufted rug has a brown jute backing. Biggest risk?
Goal: Every existing condition documented and every color tested before cleaning. The inspection is your protection.

Pre-Inspection Checklist

Front and back, in good light. Tap to check off.

  • Measure and photograph the whole rug, front and back
  • Construction and fiber identified — pile and foundation
  • Wear — thin areas, exposed knots, worn ends and sides
  • Moth damage — bare patches, grazed pile, webbing or larvae, especially under furniture and on the back
  • Dry rot — gently fold the foundation; cracking or stiffness means weak cotton
  • Pet urine — check with a UV light, front and back; note odor
  • Existing dye bleed, fading, stains — note location
  • Painted areas — worn spots touched up with ink or dye; they may run
  • Previous repairs, holes, loose sides (selvedges), damaged fringe
  • Customer signs off on the documented condition and any risks

Colorfastness Test

Test every color, especially reds, dark blues and blacks. One bleeding color can ruin the whole rug.

  1. 1Dampen a white cotton towel with the actual cleaning solution at working dilution
  2. 2Press firmly on each color for about 30 seconds
  3. 3Check the towel. Any color transfer = the dye is not stable
  4. 4Check the fringe too — color moving into it is how bleed usually shows up first
If it bleeds: don't clean it the normal way. Options are a dye-stabilizing acid rinse, cool water and very fast drying — or refer it to a rug specialist. Document the result and tell the customer before you start.

In-Plant vs. On-Location

  • In-plant is the standard for Oriental rugs. You can dust thoroughly, wash both sides, rinse fully and control drying
  • On-location only for sound, colorfast wool or synthetic rugs with no urine — using a low-moisture method
  • Never wet-clean a rug on top of hardwood or wall-to-wall carpet — moisture and dye transfer damage the floor underneath
  • Urine, dye bleed, silk, viscose, dry rot or heavy soil → take it to the plant or refer it

Pop Quiz · Inspect & Test

1. You fold the rug's foundation and hear cracking. What does that indicate?
2. What do you use to test colorfastness?
3. Best tool for finding pet urine in a rug?
Goal: Remove dry soil first, wash gently with wool-safe chemistry, rinse fully, dry fast.

Which Method?

Pick the method after inspection. When in doubt, go one level more careful.

MethodUse when
Top-DownRug in good condition, light to moderate soil, routine maintenance cleaning
Full In-Plant WashHeavy soil, spills, fringe work, or the rug needs a deep wash
Full SubmersionHeavy / saturated urine — Rug Restore soak
ReferSilk, viscose, dry rot, severe dye bleed or damage
Maintenance cleaning

Top-Down Method

Our standard maintenance method for area rugs that are not heavily damaged or soiled. The rug is dusted, then cleaned with the truck mount on both sides.

1
Identify construction, backing and fiber
Identify and Backings tabs. Colorfastness test every color. If the rug is damaged, tufted with failing latex, or has heavy urine → pick another method
2
Pre-vacuum
Vacuum the face thoroughly to remove loose soil
3
Dust with the Rug Badger
Flip the rug face down and run the Rug Badger over the back. The vibration shakes embedded grit out of the pile. Flip back and vacuum up the released soil
4
Apply the cleaner
Oriental Rug Shampoo (8 oz/gal) or the right prespray for the fiber. Work it in gently with the nap
5
Clean with the truck mount — front
Extract with the nap. Keep heat moderate on wool; add dry passes
6
Flip and clean the back
Clean and extract the back side too, then flip face up for a final dry pass and groom
7
Dry
Drying room with air movers and dehumidifiers — or outside in the sun when the temperature and relative humidity allow
Sun drying: only on warm, low-humidity days. Watch sensitive dyes — long sun exposure can fade them. Keep the rug off the ground, flip it so both sides dry, and bring it in as soon as it's fully dry. If rain or high humidity is coming, use the drying room.

Pop Quiz · Top-Down

1. The Top-Down Method is best for…
2. How do you use the Rug Badger?
3. Which sides get cleaned with the truck mount?

In-Plant Full Wash Sequence

1
Dust — remove dry soil
Hand-knotted rugs hold a surprising amount of grit deep in the pile. Dust from the back (vibration or beating), then vacuum both sides. Wetting grit turns it into mud
2
Pre-treat spots and urine
Spots: Spotting module. Urine: Urine Neutralizer (1:4) flood, dwell ~10 min, extract. USOR only on synthetics
3
Wash with Oriental Rug Shampoo
8 oz per gallon (16:1). Cool to lukewarm water, soft brush or low-speed agitation, working with the nap. No high-alkaline cleaners, no chlorine
4
Clean the fringe separately
Cotton fringe by hand with a gentle brush. Don't pull or scrub hard — the fringe is the rug's structure
5
Rinse thoroughly — finish with an acid rinse
Removes detergent residue, helps stabilize dyes and prevents browning
6
Extract water
Rug wringer, centrifuge or extraction. The more water out now, the lower the risk of bleed and browning
7
Protect and groom with the nap
Apply Maxim (1:2 — Maxim Advanced for Wool on wool) evenly, then groom. Sets the pile and evens the appearance
8
Dry fast
Hang or lay flat with strong airflow and dehumidification. Aim for dry within about 24 hours — slow drying causes bleed, browning and odor
9
Final inspection and wrap
Check both sides, re-groom, comb fringe, roll (never fold) and wrap for delivery
In-plant wash floorRoom to dust, wash both sides, rinse and control drying.
Full washGentle agitation with the nap, plenty of rinse water.
Heavy urine · In-plant

Full Submersion Method — Rug Restore

For rugs saturated with pet urine where spot treatment and flooding won't reach the contamination. The rug soaks fully submerged in Rug Restore solution so it reaches every knot, the foundation and the fringe.

Good candidates
  • Hand-knotted wool and machine-woven rugs
  • Water-cleanable synthetic rugs with no latex backing
  • Rugs that passed the colorfastness test with Rug Restore solution
Do not submerge
  • Hand-tufted or machine-tufted rugs — soaking destroys the latex and traps urine between backings
  • Viscose / art silk, jute, or dry-rotted foundations
  • Rugs that bleed in the pre-test
  • Silk — specialist only
Process
1
Inspect, UV map, and test
Photograph the urine areas under UV. Test every color with the Rug Restore solution — urine makes dyes unstable. Get customer sign-off
2
Dust and vacuum first
Remove dry soil before the rug goes in the water
3
Mix Rug Restore
Per the label — about 1 gallon to 15–25 gallons of water. Enough solution to fully cover the rolled rug
4
Roll and submerge
Roll the rug and place it in a sealed bag or in the pond. Weigh it down so the whole rug stays under the solution
5
Soak 8–12 hours
Sometimes longer on heavy contamination. Label the rug with the start time
6
Rinse with fresh water
Unroll and flush both sides until all treatment is rinsed off — rinse water runs clear with no slickness
7
Clean the rug normally
Full wash with Oriental Rug Shampoo, rinse, fringe by hand
8
Extract with the truck mount — both sides
Get out as much water as possible before drying
9
Drying room until fully dry
Air movers, plus dehumidifiers if needed. Check both sides and the fringe before rolling. Groom and apply Maxim
Set expectations: submersion removes the odor source, but urine can permanently change dye colors. Stains may lighten, not disappear. Say it before the rug goes in the water.

Pop Quiz · Submersion

1. How long does a heavy urine rug soak in Rug Restore?
2. Which rug should NOT be submerged?
3. After the soak, what comes next?

On-Location Method (when appropriate)

  1. 1Confirm it passes inspection: colorfast, no urine, sound foundation, wool or synthetic
  2. 2Move the rug off the finished floor, or protect the floor with plastic and elevate the rug
  3. 3Vacuum thoroughly, both sides if possible
  4. 4Wool-safe pre-spray, light agitation with the nap
  5. 5Low-moisture extraction with an acid rinse, extra dry passes
  6. 6Groom, air movers, and keep it off the floor until dry

Pop Quiz · Clean

1. What is the first step of an in-plant rug wash?
2. Why finish with an acid rinse?
3. What is the biggest danger of slow drying?
Goal: Right chemical, right fiber, right dilution. Read the label on the jug in your truck — it wins over this page.

Oriental Rug Shampoo

Chemspec
Wool-safeNeutral pHCleaner
Use for
Main wash / shampoo for wool, cotton and synthetic rugs
Dilution
8 oz per gallon (16:1) — rotary / rinse extraction
16 oz per gallon (8:1) — dry foam machines
How
Vacuum both sides → apply → agitate with soft brush, with the nap → rinse thoroughly
Rinse
Finish with an acid / textile rinse
Test first: still do a colorfastness test on every color, especially natural-dyed rugs.

Urine Neutralizer

Bridgepoint
Wool OK*Acidic pH 2.8–3.5Urine step 1
Use for
Decontaminating urine — dissolves the alkaline urine salts that cause odor
Dilution
1 part : 4 parts water
How
Flood the contaminated area (front and back, into the foundation) → dwell about 10 min → extract. Rinse, rinse, rinse
Works with
Water Claw / flood tools; follow with USOR on synthetics only
*Urine makes dyes unstable. Colorfastness test on every color in the urine area before flooding.

USOR (Urine Stain & Odor Remover)

TMF
NOT for woolSynthetics onlypH ~6
Use for
Urine stain and odor on synthetic rugs — nylon, polyester, olefin
How
Apply to the stain after neutralizing and extracting; also used as a prespray booster. Mist on after spot removal to prevent wicking
Watch
Peroxide-based — can lighten dyes. Test colorfastness first
Label says: Not recommended for wool. Never use it on a wool Oriental or silk rug. Wool urine = Urine Neutralizer + in-plant wash.

Maxim Protector

Bridgepoint
Final step1:2 dilutionWool version available
Use for
Stain and soil protection after cleaning
Which one
Maxim Advanced for Wool on wool rugs (pH ~5) · Maxim Advanced on synthetics
Dilution
1 part : 2 parts water
How
Apply evenly to the freshly cleaned rug with a quality sprayer, groom it in with the nap, then dry
Sell it
Protector buys time on spills — it doesn't make a rug stain-proof
Skip it on a rug that showed dye bleeding in the pre-test unless the label says it's safe for bleeders.

Rug Restore

Pro's Choice · Rug Restorer
Wool OKAcidic pH ~3Submersion
Use for
Heavy, saturated pet urine — full submersion soak
Dilution
About 1 gallon to 15–25 gallons of water (per label)
How
Roll rug → sealed bag or pond → fully submerged 8–12 hrs → fresh-water rinse until clear → normal wash → extract both sides → drying room
Details
See Clean tab → Full Submersion Method
Test first: colorfastness with the actual solution. Never submerge tufted, viscose, jute or dry-rotted rugs.

Pet Urine — Which Chemical When

RugUrine plan
Wool OrientalUV inspect → colorfastness test → Urine Neutralizer flood & extract → full wash with Oriental Rug Shampoo → rinse → dry fast → Maxim for Wool
SyntheticUrine Neutralizer → extract → USOR for remaining stain → rinse → dry → Maxim
Heavy / saturated urineFull submersion in Rug Restore 8–12 hrs → fresh-water rinse → normal wash → extract → drying room (hand-knotted & machine-woven only)
Hand-tuftedUrine trapped between backings. Neutralizer with limited moisture, set expectations — may not fully decontaminate
Silk / viscoseRefer to a rug specialist
The bottle drawings are illustrations for quick recognition, not the actual labels. Send photos of the real jugs from the truck and I'll swap them in.

Pop Quiz · Chemicals

1. A wool Oriental has pet urine. Which chemical do you NOT use?
2. Oriental Rug Shampoo dilution for rotary shampoo?
3. Which Maxim goes on a wool rug?
4. Urine Neutralizer works by…
Goal: Recognize problems early, explain them honestly, and know when to refer.

Common Problems

Dye bleeding
Unstable dyes move into lighter areas and the fringe — worse with heat, alkalinity and slow drying
Test every color. If it runs: cool water, acid rinse, fast drying. Severe bleed → specialist dye-migration correction
Cellulosic browning
Brown or yellow discoloration from cotton or jute when over-wet, alkaline, or slow-drying
Low moisture, acid rinse, fast drying. Treat with an acidic browning treatment
Pet urine
Can damage dyes and fibers permanently; odor returns when damp
UV inspection, disclose up front, in-plant decontamination soak. Some color loss may be permanent
Moth damage
Larvae eat wool pile and foundation, often under furniture or on the back
Document it, clean thoroughly, recommend repair and moth treatment
Dry rot
Cotton foundation weakened by moisture over time — can crack or tear during cleaning
Document, handle with extreme care, refer for repair assessment before washing
Latex breakdown (hand-tufted)
Backing delaminates, sheds powder, smells, stiffens or ripples
Very low moisture, no heat. Warn the customer it may be near end of life
Shrinkage
Cotton foundations and flatweaves can shrink when wet
Flag before cleaning, minimize moisture, dry flat, block if needed
Viscose distortion
Pile flattens, mats, yellows or develops water marks
Treat as high risk. Minimal moisture or refer. Set expectations in writing
Fringe yellowing / wear
Cotton fringe browns and frays
Gentle hand cleaning, brightener if compatible. Repair or re-fringing is a separate service
The Never List
  • Clean a rug without testing every color
  • Use chlorine bleach or high-alkaline cleaners on wool or silk
  • Use hot water on a rug with unstable dyes
  • Wet-clean a rug on top of hardwood or wall-to-wall carpet
  • Pull, cut or scrub hard on the fringe
  • Fold a rug for transport or storage — roll it
  • Let a rug dry slowly in a closed room
  • Promise that urine, bleed or wear will “come out”
  • Treat viscose, silk or dry-rotted rugs like wool
  • Use USOR on wool — the label says not recommended
  • Flood or soak a hand-tufted rug
Goal: Eight scenario questions. 7 of 8 to sign off on rug basics.

2. The red in a rug transfers to your test towel. Best move?

4. The fringe turned brown after another company cleaned it. Most likely cause?

6. Which direction do you wash, extract and groom a hand-knotted rug?
7. How should a clean rug be prepared for delivery?

Modules / Water Damage

Water Damage Restoration

ANSI/IICRC S500 · Mold assessment (BSR/IICRC S530) · S520 conditions.
ANSI/IICRC S500

Every water job starts with two calls: Category and Class

Category tells you how contaminated the water is. Class tells you how much water you have to dry.

Water Categories — Contamination

Category decides your PPE, what you can save, and what must be removed.

1
Clean water
Sanitary source, no substantial risk if exposed
Broken supply line · water heater · tub overflow (clean) · ice maker line
2
Significant contamination
Can cause discomfort or sickness if exposed or consumed
Washing machine / dishwasher discharge · toilet overflow with urine (no feces) · aquarium · waterbed
3
Grossly contaminated
Can contain pathogens and toxic agents — serious health risk
Sewage · toilet backflow from beyond the trap · rising flood water from rivers or sea · wind-driven rain from hurricanes and tropical storms
Category 1 exampleWater heater or supply-line leak — clean at the source.
Category 3 exampleHurricane and rising flood water. On the Emerald Coast, storm water is Cat 3.

Water Gets Worse — Category Can Change

  • Clean water that sits, warms up, or runs through soil, carpet, or building materials degrades to Cat 2 and then Cat 3
  • Categorize by what's there when you arrive, not just the source
  • Never downgrade a category because of how the water looks

Classes — How Much Water to Evaporate

Class estimates the evaporation load, based on how much wet, porous material is in the space (floor + walls + ceiling).

1Least

Wet porous materials under about 5% of the combined surface area. Mostly low-porosity materials.

2Significant

Wet porous materials about 5–40% of the combined surface area. Carpet, pad, lower walls.

3Greatest

Wet porous materials over 40% — often water from above: ceilings, walls, insulation, carpet.

4Deeply held water

Water bound in low-evaporation materials — hardwood, plaster, concrete, masonry, crawlspaces. Specialty drying, longer times.

Class definitions were refined in recent S500 editions. Always use the current edition your company trains on for the exact wording and equipment calculations.

Pop Quiz · Category & Class

1. A dishwasher overflowed into the kitchen. Category?
2. Hurricane wind-driven rain came through the windows. Category?
3. A supply-line leak sat for several days in a warm house before anyone found it. What do you consider?
4. Water in plaster walls, concrete and hardwood — deeply held. Class?
Goal: Nobody gets hurt, the source is stopped, and every wet area is found and documented before equipment goes down.
Stop — check before you walk in
  • Electrical: standing water near outlets, panels or cords — shut power to affected areas before entering
  • Structural: sagging ceilings (water pooled above), soft floors, collapsed materials
  • Slip and trip: wet hard floors, cords, debris
  • Category 3: full PPE before entry — respirator, gloves, eye protection, protective suit, boots
  • Lead and asbestos: older homes (pre-1978 paint, older ceiling texture, flooring, drywall mud) — test before demolition
  • Gas, sharps, chemicals, pests and confined spaces like crawlspaces

Initial Inspection Checklist

Tap to check off.

  • Source of water stopped — or plumber / roofer called
  • Safety hazards checked and controlled
  • Category determined — and when the loss happened
  • Moisture mapped — find the edges of the wet area with meters, beyond what you can see
  • Class estimated for each affected area
  • Materials identified — carpet & pad, drywall, baseboard, cabinets, hardwood, subfloor
  • Psychrometric readings — outside, affected area, unaffected area
  • Pre-existing damage and mold photographed and noted
  • Photos of source, every room, moisture readings
  • Work authorization signed; scope explained to the customer

Documentation Wins Claims

  • Moisture map of every room with reading locations
  • Daily logs: material readings, temperature, RH, GPP inside, outside, and at the dehumidifier exhaust
  • Equipment log — what is placed where, and when it's added or removed
  • Photos at arrival, during removal, during drying, and at completion
  • If it isn't documented, it didn't happen — for the customer and the insurance adjuster

Pop Quiz · Safety & Inspect

1. Standing water is near an outlet. First move?
2. The ceiling is sagging and bulging. What does that mean?
3. How do you find the edges of the wet area?
Goal: Understand why drying works so you can set up a balanced system — not just line up equipment.

The Principles of Drying

1
Remove the water
Extraction removes liquid water far more efficiently than any dehumidifier can evaporate it
Rule: extract thoroughly first — every gallon you extract is a gallon you don't have to dry
2
Evaporation
Air movers sweep moist air off wet surfaces so more water can evaporate
Rule: high-velocity air across the wet surface, not just blowing into the room
3
Dehumidification
Removes the evaporated moisture from the air before it goes back into materials
Rule: evaporation without dehumidification = high humidity, secondary damage and mold
4
Temperature control
Warm materials and air speed evaporation; keep the space in the range your dehumidifiers work best
Rule: Florida AC can help or hurt — manage it on purpose

Psychrometry — The Science of Air and Moisture

TermWhat it meansWhy you care
Relative Humidity (RH)How full the air is of moisture, as a %, at its current temperatureChanges with temperature — not enough on its own
Grains per Pound (GPP)Actual amount of water in the air (humidity ratio)The number to track. Compare affected vs. unaffected vs. outside
Dew PointTemperature at which moisture condensesCold surfaces below dew point get wet — condensation and mold
Vapor PressureMoisture moves from high (wet) to low (dry)Dry air near wet materials pulls moisture out
Dry StandardMoisture level of similar unaffected materials in the same buildingYour drying goal — document it on day one
Read the dehumidifier: the GPP coming out of the exhaust should be clearly lower than the GPP in the room. If there's little difference, the unit isn't pulling water — check the temperature, filter, and placement.

Secondary Damage — Why Speed Matters

  • Mold growth can begin within about 24–48 hours in warm, humid conditions — normal most of the year on the Gulf Coast
  • High humidity alone damages materials that never touched water — swelling, cupping, delamination, odor
  • Drywall wicks water upward; hardwood cups; laminate and LVP trap water underneath

Pop Quiz · Drying Science

1. Most efficient way to remove water from a building?
2. Which reading tells you the actual amount of water in the air?
3. What is the “dry standard”?
4. Air movers running without dehumidifiers will…
Goal: Use the right tool to find water, measure drying, and move moisture out of the building.

Measuring Tools

Pinless meter
Non-penetrating
Fast scans to find the wet edges — no holes
Pin meter
Penetrating
Actual moisture content in wood, drywall, baseboard
Thermo-hygrometer
Air readings
Temperature, RH → GPP and dew point
  • Thermal (infrared) camera shows temperature differences, not moisture. Evaporating water is cooler, so it points you to likely wet areas — always confirm with a moisture meter
  • Take readings in the same spots every day and mark them on the moisture map
  • Measure an unaffected area of the same material for your dry standard
Short training · ~5 min

Thermal Imaging

A thermal (infrared) camera measures surface temperature. Water evaporating from a material cools it, so wet areas usually show up cooler than dry areas around them.

It does not see moisture and it does not see through walls. It shows temperature patterns that point you to where to use your moisture meter.

Reading the Image — Real vs. False

Simulated camera views. Purple/blue = cooler, orange/yellow = warmer.

Wet drywallIrregular cool blotch rising from the floor, often with a wavy "tide line." Confirm with meter.
AC vent — not waterCool fan shape spreading from a supply vent. Turn off the HVAC and re-scan.
Window & corners — not waterStraight edges, windows, exterior corners and missing insulation read cool.

How to Scan

  1. 1Scan on arrival before moving furniture or setting equipment. Heat prints from people, furniture and sunlight can confuse the image
  2. 2Make sure there's a temperature difference. If everything reads the same, run the HVAC or wait — a flat image doesn't mean dry
  3. 3Scan the whole room — walls, ceiling, floor, baseboards, around windows, doors, tubs, sinks, dishwashers and water heaters, plus rooms next door and below
  4. 4Hold the camera square to the surface, not at a sharp angle — shiny surfaces and metal reflect heat and give false readings
  5. 5Narrow the temperature span so small differences stand out. Keep the same color palette for the whole job
  6. 6Confirm every cool area with a moisture meter, then mark it on the moisture map
  7. 7Save a thermal + regular photo of each area with the meter reading. Re-scan daily — cool areas shrinking shows the job is drying

Common False Readings

  • AC supply vents, drafts, and return air
  • Windows, exterior walls, corners and missing insulation
  • Cold water pipes and plumbing walls
  • Reflections from glossy paint, tile, glass, mirrors and metal
  • Heat prints — where furniture, a pet or a person just was
  • Sunlight warming one side of a room
Never report moisture, or tell a customer "it's dry," from the thermal camera alone. Moisture meter readings are what go in the file.

Pop Quiz · Thermal Imaging

1. What does a thermal camera actually measure?
2. You see a cool area on the wall. What's next?
3. A cool fan-shaped pattern spreads down from a ceiling vent. Most likely?
4. The whole room reads the same temperature. What does that mean?

Drying Equipment

Air movers
Job
High-velocity air across wet surfaces to speed evaporation
Watch
Never blow on visible mold growth — it spreads spores. Secure cords
LGR dehumidifiers
Job
Low Grain Refrigerant — pull the air down to low GPP. The workhorse for most residential jobs
Watch
Empty or route the drain hose; check exhaust GPP daily
Conventional refrigerant dehumidifiers
Job
Work well while the air is very wet
Watch
Lose efficiency as the air gets drier — switch to LGR
Desiccant dehumidifiers
Job
Very dry air; good for low temperatures, hardwood, and Class 4 materials
Watch
Need proper ducting and exhaust of wet air
HEPA air scrubbers
Job
Capture particles during Cat 2 / Cat 3 work and demolition
Watch
Set up for containment or negative pressure when needed
Specialty drying
Job
Floor mats and wall-cavity injection for hardwood and Class 4 materials
Watch
Monitor closely — hardwood can over-dry and crack
DehumidifierResidential unit shown. On jobs we use commercial LGR units.

Air Mover Placement

  • Place air movers along the affected walls, snout close to the wall, all angled the same direction to create a circular air pattern
  • Focus air on the wettest materials — wall bottoms, wet carpet, cabinet toe kicks
  • Size air movers and dehumidifiers using the S500 calculation / your drying software, then adjust daily from your readings
  • Close the drying area (doors, windows) so the dehumidifiers work on a controlled space

Pop Quiz · Equipment

1. A thermal camera shows a cold spot on a wall. What do you do?
2. The air is getting drier and your conventional dehumidifier is pulling almost nothing. Why?
3. How should air movers be placed?
Goal: Follow the same sequence on every loss — from the first call to the final dry reading.

Water Loss Sequence

1
Respond fast
Get cause, time of loss, category clues and access info on the call. Fast response prevents secondary damage
2
Safety & stop the source
Electrical, structural, PPE for the category. Water shut off or source controlled
3
Inspect, map & document
Category, class, moisture map, psychrometric readings, photos, work authorization
4
Protect contents
Move, block and pad furniture legs, or pack out. Protect unaffected areas
5
Extract
Remove as much water as possible — truck mount, weighted extraction on carpet, pumps for standing water
6
Remove what can't be saved
Based on category and material — see table below. Flood cut drywall above the wet line when needed
7
Clean & treat
Clean contaminated surfaces. Apply antimicrobial where appropriate (Cat 2/3) after cleaning, per label
8
Set the drying system
Air movers, dehumidifiers, air scrubbers, specialty drying — balanced for the class
9
Monitor daily
Same reading points, psychrometrics, adjust equipment, document everything
10
Dry standard reached
Materials match unaffected readings. Final photos and readings, remove equipment, hand off for rebuild

Save or Remove? — By Category

MaterialCat 1Cat 2Cat 3
CarpetUsually dry in placeClean & dry — often salvageableRemove & discard
Carpet padOften dried in placeGenerally removedRemove & discard
DrywallDry if structurally soundEvaluate; remove if heavily wetRemove above the wet line (flood cut)
InsulationEvaluateUsually removeRemove
HardwoodSpecialty dryingClean, treat, specialty dryEvaluate — often removed
Carpet & padPad soaks up and holds contamination.
Flood cutDrywall cut in a straight line above the wet line.
Cat 3 demolitionRemove contaminated porous materials with PPE and containment.
This table is a field starting point. Final decisions depend on the job, the customer, the adjuster, and the current S500 — document why each item was saved or removed.

Pop Quiz · Job Process

1. Sewage backup soaked carpet and pad. What happens to them?
2. When is antimicrobial applied?
3. How do you know the job is dry?
Goal: Recognize suspected mold, stop before you make it worse, and get it properly assessed.

What the Standards Cover

  • BSR/IICRC S530 — the new standard (still in development) for assessing structures suspected of mold contamination. The assessment is done by a qualified Indoor Environmental Professional (IEP): inspection, sampling plan, and a report
  • ANSI/IICRC S520 — the mold remediation standard, including the Conditions used to describe contamination
  • Water techs don't diagnose mold. Our job is to recognize it, stop, protect, document and report

Mold Conditions (S520)

1
Normal fungal ecology
The indoor environment has the normal mold background you'd expect for that area
2
Settled spores
Area contaminated with settled spores from a Condition 3 area — may include traces of growth
3
Actual growth
Actual mold growth, active or dormant, visible or hidden

Signs of Suspected Mold

Growth at wall baseCommon after water wicks up drywall.
Ceiling growthSpreads fast in hot, humid, closed homes after storms.
  • Visible growth, fuzzy or spotted discoloration, or staining that keeps spreading
  • Musty odor, especially in closed rooms, cabinets and wall cavities
  • Water that sat more than 24–48 hours before we arrived
  • Occupant complaints — allergy symptoms, breathing problems

When You Suspect Mold — Stop Rule

  1. 1Stop. Don't disturb it — no demo, no scrubbing, no air movers blowing on it
  2. 2Protect yourself (respirator, gloves, eye protection) and the rest of the home — close the area off
  3. 3Document with photos, location, size and moisture readings
  4. 4Call the crew lead / office. The customer may need an IEP assessment before remediation
  5. 5Remediation follows S520: containment, HEPA air filtration, removal of contaminated materials, cleaning, and verification
Never
  • Blow air movers across visible mold growth
  • Tell the customer "it's just a little mold" — you can't diagnose it
  • Spray bleach and call it fixed
  • Tear out moldy materials without containment

Pop Quiz · Mold

1. You find visible mold at the base of a wall. What do you do first?
2. Who performs the assessment described in S530?
3. Condition 3 means…

This module is a field summary — always follow the current editions, your company procedures, and manufacturer labels.

Modules / Upholstery

Upholstery Cleaning

Inspect · Test · Choose · Clean · Verify. Supervisor approval still required.
The field rule
Inspect the whole piece, test the proposed method, and check the test again when dry. If the result changes the fabric, stop and call the lead.
Before chemistry: inspect the entire piece.

Identify the Fabric

Read the furniture label and care code. Check fiber claims, face fabric, backing, seams, trim, cushion inserts and accessible construction. Appearance alone cannot confirm fiber content.

Care Codes

W
Water-basedClean with a specified water-based cleaner
S
SolventSpecified solvent cleaning only — no water-based cleaning
WS
EitherMay allow either specified type (also shown as SW)
X
Vacuum onlyVacuum or light brushing only — no wet or solvent cleaning
Read the full maker instructions. A code does not override a failed fabric test.

Record What's Already There

Tap to check off.

  • Label and care code photographed
  • Fading and sun damage
  • Worn edges, thin arms, loose stitching
  • Spots, rings and pile changes
  • Past cleaning attempts — rings, stiffness, residue
  • Customer expectations discussed before promising results
Hidden area · actual working solution. Test before cleaning.

Four Tests

1
Dry transfer
Gently rub a concealed area with a clean white towel. Check both towel and fabric for color or abrasion
2
Wet colorfastness
Test the intended product at its labeled dilution in a small hidden area. Press with a white towel; inspect each color and contrasting trim
3
Dry-result check
Let the test area dry. Look for rings, browning, shrinkage, stiffness, pile change or backing bleed
4
Fiber evidence
Combine the label, construction and available samples. A burn result alone cannot prove an exact fiber, especially in blends or finished textiles

Burn-Test Sample — Upholstery Rules

A trained, authorized technician may open an accessible cushion zipper and clip a tiny concealed surplus thread or allowance from the same face fabric.

  • Avoid the structural seam, lining, ticking, batting, barrier and zipper tape
  • Photograph the location and close the zipper
  • Test the detached sample away from the furniture using the approved fire setup
  • No matching surplus available? Ask the lead

The decision point: match the method to the evidence.

Pick the Method

Synthetic upholstery
Method
Hot water extraction — Prochem Upholstery Pre-Spray (pH 8.5) → rinse & extract
Needs
Passed tests and a W or WS code
Natural and sensitive textiles
Method
Follow the label and the successful test. Often low-moisture foam with Fine Fabric Shampoo (pH 6.0)
Needs
Fusion natural-fiber release when required — a signature never makes a failed test safe
S code or X code
Method
S: specified solvent method only. X: vacuum / light brushing only
Needs
Call the lead before quoting

Oily Contact Areas

  • Headrest / neck — hair products and body oil
  • Armrests — hand and body oils
  • Front edge and leg contact — soil and abrasion
  • Solvent-emulsifying chemistry may help oily soil when the product and fabric method allow. Work gently around worn fabric
Stop and call the lead
  • Dye transfer or a ring after drying
  • Browning, shrinkage or texture change
  • Unknown backing, delicate pile or viscose concerns
  • Label and test disagree
  • Odor source inside the cushion
Measure · protect · control moisture. Mix safely and clean in sections.

Dilution Quick Table

ProductPer 1 gal waterPer 32 oz water
Upholstery Pre-Spray (pump)8 fl oz2 fl oz
Fine Fabric Shampoo3–5 fl oz0.75–1.25 fl oz
Citrus Pro (booster)½–1 fl oz per gallon of mixed RTU prespray — not per gallon of water
Pump-sprayer math: label dose × water volume ÷ 128 fl oz. One US gallon = 128 fl oz. Measure liquid volume, not weight.

Cleaning Sequence — Synthetic (Hot Water Extraction)

  1. 1Protect nearby finishes, floors and walls. Vacuum dry soil first — seams, crevices, under cushions
  2. 2Apply Upholstery Pre-Spray — only as much as the method needs. Oily areas first (headrest, arms, front edge)
  3. 3Agitate gently with an upholstery brush, working in sections
  4. 4Rinse & extract with the upholstery tool and an All Fiber Rinse. Recover moisture promptly — don't saturate the insert
  5. 5Extra dry passes, groom the fabric, set up airflow

Cleaning Sequence — Low-Moisture Foam (Fine Fabric Shampoo)

  1. 1Vacuum. Mix 3–5 oz per gallon of water
  2. 2Apply with a natural sponge or horsehair brush in even strokes
  3. 3Scrub gently to work up a foam, overlapping the previous section
  4. 4Wipe with a clean towel to absorb solution and soil
  5. 5Extract or post-spray with All Fiber Rinse to soften the fabric and inhibit browning. Align the pile and dry
Chemical safety
  • Read the current label and SDS; gloves and eye protection; ventilate
  • Measure with a clean graduated device and label the working container
  • Never mix unrelated chemicals or add bleach
  • Don't mix an alkaline prespray with an acidic shampoo to "balance" pH
  • Keep chemicals away from food, children, pets and ignition sources
Finish the job: dry, compare, and communicate.

Final Walkthrough

  • Extra recovery passes made; cushions set securely; airflow across damp surfaces
  • Compared with before photos
  • Checked for rings, dye movement, residue, tool marks, texture change and remaining moisture
  • Told the customer what improved, what remains, any limits, and when they can use it
  • Concerns documented before leaving
Never promise full odor removal when the source may be in the cushion insert. Agree on the treatment scope with the customer and lead.
